The paper makes a strong mechanistic claim — "optimization gains compounded only when regression control was built into the optimization loop" (Abstract) and claims "regression control must live inside the search loop" (Section 1.4) — yet its own method table says the compared systems also "differ in search space, proposer model, and whether regression control is enforced during search" (Table 2). The paper further admits it "cannot fully distinguish 'generalization filter' from other explanations" (Section 6.6), so the design does not isolate regression control causally.

Table 2 reveals that the evaluated methods differ not just in regression handling, but also in search space and proposer model (e.g., RELAI-VCL searches over 'Prompt, tool, workflow, memory, skill, code' while GEPA searches 'Prompts'), so the experimental design does not isolate in-loop regression control as the sole causal factor.

judge_panel.reason: The paper reports only point estimates throughout (e.g., '79.2%', '72.7%') with no confidence intervals, bootstrap intervals, variance over seeds, or per-task breakdowns, and Section 3.3 notes only that 'every task is evaluated twice per agent,' which is an extremely small number of trials providing no basis for statistical uncertainty quantification.

The evaluation is based on very few repeated measurements — "Every task is evaluated twice per agent" (Section 3.3) — and the paper reports only point estimates in Tables 4–8 such as "Baseline 62.5%, GEPA 70.8%, Meta Harness 66.6%, RELAI-VCL 79.2%" without any confidence intervals, variance estimates, or seed sensitivity. Strong statements like "RELAI-VCL is the only method that leads at every one of the four evaluated stages" (Section 6.5) are therefore unsupported by uncertainty quantification.

The paper reports exact percentages based on 2 trials per task (Section 3.3) for 12 to 22 tasks, but provides no confidence intervals, variance across runs, or statistical significance tests to support its comparative claims.
